name: Arsik Dengke Mas
description: The absolute signature cultural dish of the Batak people. It features fresh gold fish (Mas) simmered in a complex paste of indigenous spices, specifically andaliman peppercorns and kincong.
history: Traditionally served during sacred life-cycle ceremonies (weddings, births, achievements) to represent long life, health, and familial harmony.
preparation: Clean the gold fish, leaving the scales intact representing armor/strength.
Blend turmeric, ginger, chili, garlic, shallot, and lots of andaliman to form a thick golden spice paste.
Line the bottom of a wok with layers of fresh galangal, lemongrass, torch ginger, and Batak chives.
Lay the fish on top, rubbing it with the spice paste.
Add water and simmer slowly on low fire until the broth thickens and turns into a rich, aromatic golden glaze.

name: Dengke Mas Na Niura
description: Often referred to as the "Batak Sushi." This legendary dish features raw gold fish (or lake carp) cured purely with acidic citrus juices and heavily flavored with roasted spices like andaliman.
history: In ancient times, Dengke Na Niura was an exclusive royal culinary delicacy reserved solely for Batak kings. Over time, it became a highly sought-after cultural masterpiece for special gatherings.
preparation: Carefully fillet the fresh gold fish or tilapia and thoroughly pat dry.
Squeeze Asam Jungga juice over the fish fillets. The highly acidic citrus acts as a chemical cooking agent, denaturing the proteins and "cooking" the fish raw.
Let the fish cure in citrus for 4 to 6 hours until the flesh firms up and turns opaque.
Roast the candle-nuts, shallots, garlic, and andaliman, then grind them into a rich, buttery, savory paste.
Thoroughly coat the cured fish fillets with the spicy paste before serving cold.

name: Mie Gomak
description: The beloved "Spaghetti of the Bataks." Made using thick, chewy local wheat noodles called Mie Lidi, it is bathed in a fragrant, spicy andaliman-scented coconut curry broth, or stir-fried dry.
history: The name "Gomak" translates literally to "by hand," tracing back to the traditional method where street vendors would grab and portion the hot noodles using their hands before serving.
ingredients: Mie Lidi (Thick yellow dried wheat noodles)
preparation: Boil the thick Mie Lidi in rolling hot water until perfectly al dente, drain and coat with a dash of oil.
Sauté blended spices including shallots, garlic, turmeric, and dried chili until aromatic.
Pour in fresh coconut milk and stir constantly to prevent separation.
Add crushed andaliman, which delivers a distinct citrusy numbing sensation to the tongue.
Add greens, then serve the noodles bathed in the thick, piping hot yellow-red curry broth.

name: Saksang Batak
description: A savory, intensely spiced signature Batak pork or beef dish stewed in a rich paste of lemongrass, lime leaves, and an optional traditional thick blood sauce or coconut cream.
history: A foundational staple for all major Batak clan gatherings, traditional weddings, and custom councils, representing community solidarity and hospitality.
ingredients: Fresh Blood or thick coconut cream glaze
preparation: Dice the meat into small bite-sized cubes.
Roast and dry grind coriander, pepper, candle-nuts, and andaliman.
Sauté the ground aromatics along with crushed lemongrass, lime leaves, and turmeric leaves.
Stir in the cubed meat, cooking until it releases its natural juices.
Add water and simmer until tender. In the final minutes, stir in filtered blood or thick spiced coconut milk to glaze the meat into a dark, highly savory sauce.

name: Kue Ombus-Ombus
description: A highly delightful, sweet snack consisting of freshly steamed rice-flour dough stuffed with warm, melting palm sugar and wrapped in fragrant banana leaves.
history: Originating from Siborongborong, North Tapanuli, "Ombus" means "to blow on/huff." They are served piping hot, forcing you to blow on them before taking a sweet, steaming bite.
preparation: In a large mixing bowl, gently combine rice flour, salt, and freshly grated coconut.
Slowly moisten the flour mixture with a dash of pandan leaf water to form a crumbly dough.
Cut banana leaves into squares and roll into small cones.
Fill half of the cone with the flour mixture, place a generous spoonful of shaved palm sugar in the center, and cover with more flour.
Fold the cone securely and steam for 20-30 minutes until the sugar inside melts into syrup.
